title: Congress Holds the Court's Purse Strings, Too
hook: The judiciary doesn't get to set its own budget. In July 2026, Justices Kagan and Barrett had to go to Capitol Hill and ask for one — like any other federal agency.
key_points: Courts don't fund themselves: a legislature's power over the budget reaches even the judicial branch.
In July 2026, Justices Elena Kagan and Amy Coney Barrett testified before House and Senate subcommittees to make the Supreme Court's budget request.
The justices also used the appearance to raise the Court's security concerns to lawmakers who control its funding.
Justices testifying before Congress is rare enough to be newsworthy, but it isn't new — it happens periodically whenever the Court needs to make its case for resources.
The episode is a quiet, budgetary version of checks and balances: even the branch that reviews the other two still has to ask them for money.
content_html: The judicial branch reviews the constitutionality of what Congress and the president do — but it doesn't get to write its own check. Like every other part of the federal government, the Supreme Court depends on Congress to appropriate its budget, which means that even the justices occasionally have to show up and ask for money.
extra_html: That happened in July 2026, when Justices Elena Kagan and Amy Coney Barrett testified before House and Senate subcommittees to present the Court's budget request, SCOTUSblog reported. The justices also used the rare public appearance to flag the Court's security concerns directly to the lawmakers who control its funding. It's an unusual sight — the branch that can strike down an act of Congress showing up to ask that same Congress for resources — but SCOTUSblog's Kelsey Dallas and Nora Collins frame it as part of a longer, if infrequent, history of justices testifying on Capitol Hill. It's a small but telling reminder that "separation of powers" doesn't mean total independence: budgetary control is one of the legislature's quieter but most durable checks on every other branch. (This card describes the U.S. federal judiciary specifically.)

flashcards.prompt: Why does the judicial branch have to ask Congress for its budget at all?

choices.text: The legislature's power over spending reaches every branch of government, courts included
The Supreme Court has no budget of its own and is funded case-by-case
The Constitution requires an annual vote of confidence in the judiciary

flashcards.explanation_html: Control of the budget is one of a legislature's core checks — no branch, including the courts, is exempt from needing appropriated funds.
